question: Reading a book in a moving car can make you feel sick because your eyes say you're sitting still, while another part of your body says you're moving. Which part?
topic: Car sickness and motion sickness remedies
source_excerpt: When you are in a car the vestibular system is correctly sensing the acceleration you are experiencing, but your eyes are perceiving that you are not moving.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone knows reading in the back seat makes you queasy, but most people think of it as a stomach problem. The real culprit is a disagreement between the eyes and the ear, which also explains why staring at the horizon helps.
extra.verification_notes: Sensory-conflict theory attributes reading-in-car motion sickness to the eyes signalling stillness while the inner ear (vestibular system) senses motion (https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/why-does-reading-in-a-mov).

explanation: The balance organs deep in your inner ear feel every bump and turn, and when your eyes disagree, the brain gets confused and you feel sick. Looking out at the horizon lets your eyes confirm what your ears already know.

question: The word 'nausea' comes from an Ancient Greek word for a means of transport. Which one?
topic: Car sickness and motion sickness remedies
source_excerpt: From Ancient Greek ναυσία (nausía, 'seasickness'), from ναῦς (naûs, 'ship')

extra.why_interesting: People use 'nausea' for any queasiness and never think about where it comes from. It turns out the word literally means ship-sickness, so seasickness gave its name to the whole feeling. Players can work it out through 'nautical' or 'navy'.
extra.verification_notes: Wiktionary derives nausea from Greek nausía (seasickness), from naûs 'ship'.

explanation: The Greek 'naus' meant ship, the same root as 'nautical', so nausea literally means seasickness. Sailors had the feeling long before anyone got carsick.
